knownFor.label: Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew
knownFor.note: Built when Bangkok became the capital.

knownFor.label: Never colonised
knownFor.note: Siam stayed independent as a buffer between British and French colonies.

knownFor.label: Muay Thai
knownFor.note: A traditional fighting art used in military training.

location.value: Central Thailand around Bangkok. At its greatest extent (c. 1805) its power reached the Shan States, southern Yunnan, Laos, Cambodia and the northern Malay states.

terrain.value: The Chao Phraya delta. Bangkok was built on the east bank among canals and marshland, a site chosen partly for defence against Burma.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon. The rice economy depends on the seasonal floods.
climate.source: Baker & Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed., 2014)

resources.value: Rice (which became the top export after 1855), teak, tin and sugar.

disasters.value: Seasonal floods. No major disasters are documented in the sources checked.

population.value: About 5 million in 1805, about 6 million in 1893, and 11,506,207 in 1929 (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Bangkok grew from a new capital (1782) into the dominant city and port, with a large Chinese community in Sampheng.

disease.value: Cholera epidemics occurred in the 19th century, but they are not detailed in the sources checked.

migration.value: Large Chinese immigration (traders, labourers, tax farmers). Laotian and other war captives were resettled in central Siam.

economicBase.value: Rice agriculture. A royal trade monopoly gave way to a rice-export economy after the Bowring Treaty.

tradeRoutes.value: Junk trade with China. After the Burney (1826) and Bowring (1855) treaties, open trade with Britain and then other Western powers.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is available in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: Photduang (bullet money) until 1904. The baht (tical) as coinage from 1860. The Bowring Treaty capped import duties at 3% and gave the British extraterritoriality.

inequality.value: A hierarchical sakdina system of nobles and commoners owing corvée labour, plus slaves, until Chulalongkorn’s reforms abolished slavery (completed 1905) and corvée.

governmentType.value: A mandala monarchy (1782–1892), then a centralised absolute monarchy (1892–1932). There was no legislature.

keyRulers.value: Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok, 1782–1809, founder of the Chakri dynasty). Rama III (Nangklao, 1824–1851). Mongkut (Rama IV, 1851–1868). Chulalongkorn (Rama V, 1868–1910). Prajadhipok (Rama VII, 1925–1932/35).

succession.value: Hereditary in the Chakri dynasty, with a “Front Palace” viceroy as second king until the post was abolished in 1885 after the Front Palace Crisis (1874–75).

institutions.value: Chulalongkorn’s reforms: modern ministries (1892), the provincial monthon system, the end of slavery and corvée, and modern schools and courts.

stability.value: Generally stable dynasty. A failed Palace Revolt (1912) and the Siamese Revolution of 24 June 1932, which ended absolute monarchy.

eliteConflict.value: The Front Palace Crisis (1874–75) between Chulalongkorn and the viceroy. Tensions between the royal elite and Western-educated officials and officers, which led to 1932.

armyAndTech.value: In the Nine Armies’ War (1785–86), Siam mustered 70,000 men against 144,000 Burmese. A modern army and navy were built from the late 19th century.

majorWars.value: The Nine Armies’ War with Burma (1785–86). Suppression of the Lao rebellion (1826–28). War with Vietnam over Cambodia (1841–45). The Franco-Siamese crisis (1893). Joined the First World War on the Allied side (1917).

territoryChange.value: Fell from about 1.12 million km² (1805) to about 727,000 km² (1893), as lands in Laos, Cambodia and the Malay states were ceded to France and Britain (1893–1909).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Burma, Vietnam, and later the colonial powers France and Britain. Siam balanced between Britain and France to stay independent.

inventions.value: Adopted Western technology: printing, railways, the telegraph, steamships and modern medicine, mainly under Mongkut and Chulalongkorn.
inventions.source: Baker & Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed., 2014)

scienceEducation.value: Mongkut studied Western astronomy. Modern schools and Chulalongkorn University (1917). Literacy grew in the early 20th century.
scienceEducation.source: Baker & Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed., 2014)

openness.value: Selective modernisation: opened to Western trade and ideas (1855 onwards) while keeping royal authority, which was key to avoiding colonisation.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism as the state religion, reformed by Mongkut’s Thammayut order. Hindu, Christian and Muslim minorities.

languageWriting.value: Thai (Siamese) in Thai script. Lao, Khmer, Malay and Chinese were also spoken.

artsArchitecture.value: The Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew (Emerald Buddha). Wat Arun. Royal literature such as Rama I’s version of the Ramakien.

socialStructure.value: King and royal family, nobles (khunnang), commoners (phrai) and slaves (that), until the abolition of slavery and corvée under Chulalongkorn.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to king and Buddhism. A modern Thai nationalism developed under Vajiravudh (Rama VI). The country was renamed Thailand in 1939.
sharedIdentity.source: Baker & Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed., 2014)

neighbours.value: Burma, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, the northern Malay states (Kedah, Kelantan, Terengganu, Patani), British Burma and Malaya, and French Indochina.

ideasReligions.value: Exchange with Western missionaries and diplomats. The Chinese community shaped commerce and culture.

colonisation.value: The only Southeast Asian state to keep its independence. It acted as an overlord of tributary states itself, but ceded territory to France and Britain.

riseSignals.value: Rama I rebuilt Siam after the fall of Ayutthaya (1767). A defensible new capital, victory over Burma, and control of tributary states.

peakPeriod.value: Territorial height around 1805. Modernisation peak under Chulalongkorn (1868–1910).

declineSignals.value: Colonial pressure and territorial losses (1893–1909), and the failure to make democratic reforms, which led to the 1932 revolution.

outcome.value: Transformation, not collapse. The 1932 revolution created a constitutional monarchy, and the country continues today as the Kingdom of Thailand (renamed in 1939).

sources.value: Thai royal chronicles, treaties, and British, French and missionary records. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (the article carries cleanup warnings). See also Baker & Phongpaichit (2014). Covers mainly 1782–1932; Thailand after 1932 is not yet covered in detail.

overallCertainty.value: Good for events and treaties. Early population figures are rough. The founding date is 6 or 21 April 1782 depending on the source.
